questions.stem: Which products form when an alcohol burns completely in air?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water only
options.explanation: Complete combustion converts all carbon to CO2 and all hydrogen to H2O.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide signals incomplete combustion with limited oxygen.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: Hydrogen burns to water; it is not a combustion product of the alcohol.

options.text: Carbon dioxide, water and soot
options.explanation: Soot indicates incomplete combustion, not the complete case.

questions.stem: Complete combustion of methanol requires how many oxygen molecules per methanol molecule?

options.text: Three per methanol molecule
options.explanation: That would give six oxygens per methanol, double the requirement.

options.text: One and a half, giving 2CH3OH + 3O2 in whole-number form
options.explanation: CH3OH + 1.5O2 closes the census: one carbon, four hydrogens, four oxygens each side.

options.text: One
options.explanation: One oxygen molecule cannot oxidise all four hydrogens to water and the carbon to carbon dioxide.

options.text: Two
options.explanation: Two oxygen molecules over-supplies the census by one oxygen.

questions.stem: Why are alcohols useful as fuels?

options.text: They are non-flammable liquids
options.explanation: Alcohols are flammable; that is the basis of their fuel role.

options.text: They produce carbon monoxide as their main product
options.explanation: Carbon monoxide is the incomplete-combustion product and a hazard, not the goal.

options.text: Their combustion is strongly exothermic and, when complete, gives clean products
options.explanation: Energy release plus simple products underlie the fuel use of ethanol and methanol.

options.text: They burn without needing any oxygen
options.explanation: Combustion requires oxygen; no fuel burns without it.

questions.stem: Compared with methanol, the complete combustion of propan-1-ol needs

options.text: The same oxygen per molecule, since all alcohols burn alike
options.explanation: Atom counts differ, so the oxygen demands differ.

options.text: Less oxygen, because the alcohol supplies its own oxygen atom
options.explanation: The single hydroxyl oxygen is far short of the demand from three carbons.

options.text: No oxygen at all, since alcohols self-oxidise
options.explanation: Air supplies the oxidant; the alcohol does not oxidise itself.

options.text: More oxygen per molecule, because three carbons and eight hydrogens demand more oxidation
options.explanation: More atoms per molecule means a larger oxygen coefficient in the balanced equation.

questions.stem: A yellow, sooty flame during an alcohol's burning indicates

options.text: Incomplete combustion, with insufficient oxygen producing soot and possibly carbon monoxide
options.explanation: Soot is unburnt carbon, the classic sign that oxygen supply fell short.

options.text: Complete combustion at a higher temperature
options.explanation: Complete burning gives a clean blue flame without soot.

options.text: That the alcohol has a longer carbon chain than expected
options.explanation: Chain length changes the oxygen demand but not the flame colour when oxygen is ample.

options.text: Water condensing on the flame
options.explanation: Condensed water is invisible; soot is the combustion signature.

questions.stem: State the word equation for the complete combustion of an alcohol.
questions.modelAnswer: Alcohol plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water, with the oxygen supplied from the air.

questions.stem: Name the two products of complete combustion and the condition they require.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and water form when oxygen is plentiful enough for complete burning.

questions.stem: Explain why the alcohol's own oxygen atom does not make its combustion oxygen requirement zero.
questions.modelAnswer: One hydroxyl oxygen cannot cover the many oxygen atoms needed to oxidise every carbon to carbon dioxide and every hydrogen to water, so air must still supply the balance of the oxygen demand.

questions.stem: Balance the complete combustion of ethanol in molecular form and verify the atom census.
questions.modelAnswer: C2H5OH + 3O2 gives 2CO2 + 3H2O: carbon census 2 = 2, hydrogen census 6 = 6, oxygen census 1 + 6 = 7 on the left and 4 + 3 = 7 on the right, so the equation closes exactly.

questions.stem: What is observed when phosphorus(V) chloride is added to an unknown alcohol?

options.text: A blue flame as the alcohol ignites
options.explanation: PCl5 addition does not ignite the mixture.

options.text: A vigorous reaction at room temperature releasing steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride
options.explanation: The -OH group is replaced and HCl gas escapes as misty fumes, confirming the hydroxyl group.

options.text: A slow reaction only after prolonged heating
options.explanation: The PCl5 reaction is vigorous at room temperature with no heating needed.

options.text: A red precipitate forming slowly
options.explanation: No precipitate forms; the diagnostic observation is the fumes.

questions.stem: Why can concentrated hydrochloric acid alone chlorinate a tertiary alcohol but not a primary one?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid is too weak for any alcohol
options.explanation: The acid does chlorinate tertiary alcohols, so the acid strength is sufficient there.

options.text: Primary alcohols lack a hydroxyl group
options.explanation: Primary alcohols carry the same -OH group as tertiary ones.

options.text: The tertiary pathway proceeds by a different mechanism that primary carbons cannot support
options.explanation: Tertiary carbocations are accessible for the acid route, while primary carbons lack that pathway.

options.text: Primary alcohols are too volatile for the acid route
options.explanation: Volatility is irrelevant to the mechanistic reach of the acid route.

questions.stem: In the bromination of an alcohol, the 50 percent sulfuric acid concentration matters because

options.text: Weaker acid would evaporate the potassium bromide
options.explanation: Evaporation is not the concern; bromide oxidation is.

options.text: The acid acts as the bromine source itself
options.explanation: The bromine comes from KBr; the acid generates HBr from it.

options.text: The acid catalyses the alcohol's dehydration instead
options.explanation: Dehydration is the phosphoric acid route, not this one.

options.text: Stronger acid would oxidise bromide ions to bromine, diverting the route into side products
options.explanation: Half-strength acid generates HBr cleanly; full strength sends bromide off to Br2.

questions.stem: The iodination of an alcohol requires heating under reflux because

options.text: The phosphorus-plus-iodine route is slow, so prolonged heating with everything retained is needed
options.explanation: Reflux keeps the volatile species in the mixture while the substitution crawls to completion.

options.text: Iodine gas escapes unless the condenser blocks it permanently
options.explanation: Reflux does retain volatiles, but the reason is the slow reaction needing sustained heating.

options.text: The alcohol would freeze at room temperature
options.explanation: Alcohols are liquids at room temperature; freezing is not the issue.

options.text: PI3 reacts instantly and no heating is ever used
options.explanation: The route explicitly requires heating under reflux.

questions.stem: Which inorganic compound forms as a co-product when phosphorus(III) iodide reacts with an alcohol?

options.text: Potassium sulfate
options.explanation: Potassium sulfate is the bromination pre-reaction co-product.

options.text: Phosphorous acid, H3PO3
options.explanation: The substitution hands the three iodine atoms to alcohol molecules and the phosphorus emerges as H3PO3.

options.text: Phosphoric acid, H3PO4
options.explanation: Phosphoric acid is the dehydration reagent, not this co-product.

options.text: Phosphorus(V) chloride
options.explanation: PCl5 belongs to the chlorination route entirely.

questions.stem: State the observation that identifies the -OH group using phosphorus(V) chloride.
questions.modelAnswer: Steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride are released immediately at room temperature, evidencing the hydroxyl group.

questions.stem: Name the reagents used to supply bromine and iodine in the alcohol conversions.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromination uses potassium bromide with 50 percent sulfuric acid, and iodination uses red phosphorus with iodine under reflux.

questions.stem: Explain why the bromination reaction is written as two separate equations.
questions.modelAnswer: The inorganic reagents react together first to make hydrogen bromide and potassium sulfate, and only then does the hydrogen bromide substitute the alcohol's hydroxyl group, so the chemistry splits into a generation step and a substitution step.

questions.stem: Write the two-step equations for converting butan-1-ol to 1-bromobutane and verify the atom census of the second step.
questions.modelAnswer: Step one is 2KBr + H2SO4 giving K2SO4 + 2HBr; step two is CH3CH2CH2CH2OH + HBr giving CH3CH2CH2CH2Br + H2O, whose census closes with four carbons, ten hydrogens and one oxygen on each side.

questions.stem: Which reagent dehydrates an alcohol to an alkene?

options.text: Sodium carbonate solution
options.explanation: Carbonate washes products; it does not dehydrate alcohols.

options.text: Dilute sulfuric acid at room temperature
options.explanation: The dehydration reagent is concentrated phosphoric acid with heating.

options.text: Concentrated phosphoric acid
options.explanation: Heating with concentrated H3PO4 removes water and forms the alkene.

options.text: Phosphorus(V) chloride
options.explanation: PCl5 substitutes the hydroxyl with chlorine rather than eliminating water.

questions.stem: What bonds form during the dehydration of an alcohol?

options.text: A carbon-oxygen double bond in place of the hydroxyl
options.explanation: The oxygen leaves with the water; no C=O forms in alkene products.

options.text: A carbon-halogen bond
options.explanation: Halogenation forms C-X; dehydration forms C=C.

options.text: An oxygen-oxygen bond
options.explanation: No peroxide chemistry is involved in dehydration.

options.text: A carbon-carbon double bond between the hydroxyl carbon and its neighbour
options.explanation: Eliminating water lets the adjacent carbons close into a C=C bond.

questions.stem: Why does concentrated phosphoric acid not appear in the dehydration equation?

options.text: The water formed in the reaction dilutes the concentrated acid, so the catalyst is not consumed into the stoichiometry
options.explanation: The acid serves as the dehydrating medium while the product water dilutes it.

options.text: The acid evaporates before the reaction starts
options.explanation: Phosphoric acid is not the volatile component here.

options.text: The acid is insoluble in alcohols
options.explanation: Catalysts need not dissolve; the real reason is dilution by the product water.

options.text: The acid is reduced to phosphorus during the reaction
options.explanation: No redox change befalls the acid in dehydration.

questions.stem: The dehydration of ethanol produces which alkene?

options.text: Ethane, by reduction
options.explanation: Dehydration is elimination, not reduction; no hydrogen is added.

options.text: Ethene, CH2=CH2
options.explanation: Losing water from ethanol closes a double bond between the two carbons, giving ethene.

options.text: Ethenol, with the OH still attached
options.explanation: The hydroxyl group is removed in dehydration; it cannot remain.

options.text: Ethyne, with a triple bond
options.explanation: One elimination forms a double bond, not a triple bond.

questions.stem: Dehydration of an alcohol is described as similar to the elimination reaction of a halogenoalkanes because both

options.text: Produce alcohols as their products
options.explanation: Both produce alkenes, not alcohols.

options.text: Occur only at room temperature
options.explanation: Both eliminations need heating to proceed.

options.text: Remove a small molecule across adjacent carbons to leave a C=C double bond
options.explanation: Halogenoalkanes eliminate HX and alcohols eliminate water, both closing the double bond.

options.text: Require a halogen atom to depart
options.explanation: Alcohol dehydration departs water, with no halogen involved.

questions.stem: State the equation for the dehydration of ethanol.
questions.modelAnswer: CH3CH2OH gives CH2=CH2 and H2O when heated with concentrated phosphoric acid.

questions.stem: Name the bonds broken and formed when an alcohol dehydrates.
questions.modelAnswer: The C-O bond of the hydroxyl and a C-H bond on the adjacent carbon break, while a C=C double bond forms between those carbons.

questions.stem: Explain why the water formed in dehydration is the molecule that dilutes the acid.
questions.modelAnswer: The eliminated hydroxyl and adjacent hydrogen combine into exactly the water that appears as the co-product, and that fresh water mixes into and dilutes the concentrated phosphoric acid as the reaction proceeds.

questions.stem: Predict the alkene products when butan-2-ol dehydrates and justify why more than one alkene can form.
questions.modelAnswer: The hydroxyl carbon can pair its elimination with hydrogens on either neighbouring carbon, so but-1-ene and but-2-ene both form, with the double bond closing on whichever side loses the hydrogen.
